name: Kyak
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Harley, Matthew. 2020. Aspects of the phonology and morphosyntax of Kyak, an Adamawa language of Nigeria. Language in Africa 1(3), 373-404. Moscow: Institute of Linguistics RAN. doi:10.37892/2686-8946-2020-1-3-373-404 (open access:https://iling-ran.ru/library/languageinafrica/1/LiA_3_12_Harley.pdf)
catalog_locator: §3.3 Tones, pp. 378-379, example (1) on p. 379; §3.5 Distribution, p. 381 for syllable structure.
catalog_quote: Kyak has three contrastive lexical tones, High, Low, and Falling, as shown by the minimal triplet in (1). [...] (1) a. sém ‘pot’ b. sèm ‘monkey’ c. sêm ‘servant’. One lexical oddity, [ɗə́ꜜsí] ‘face’, contains a downstepped high tone, presumably caused by a floating low tone trapped between the two high tones. Downstepped and upstepped high tones are quite common in phrases and sentences, as are phonetic mid tones, which are produced as a result of low-tone raising next to an adjacent high, among other processes, many of which are not yet well understood. In this paper, all examples are marked with surface tones, and a thorough analysis of tone sandhi is left for future research. [...] [p. 381] The vast majority of morphemes are monosyllabic with the structure CV or CVC, with both types being extremely common. Very few words have more than two syllables.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kyak is a register-tone language with three lexical tones (H, L, HL falling) plus downstep; the only description of its phonology makes no statement about word stress or accent at all (no occurrence of 'stress', 'accent' or 'prominence' in the paper). Most morphemes are monosyllabic CV/CVC, so a word-stress rule would be largely vacuous.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tonal oddity ɗə́ꜜsí 'face' with lexical downstep.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on words; sandhi/downstep at phrase level. Nothing on citation-form vs phrasal prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Harley 2020 describes Kyak [bka] as spoken at Bambuka and neighbouring towns, Karim Lamido LGA, Taraba State (endonym [kʲák]; outsiders say Kyak or Bambuka); the author states there are no known dialect differences. Same languoid as kyak1243. Moo [gwg] and Leelau [ldk] are near-mutually intelligible relatives (>90% lexical similarity) but have their own codes.

tone.summary: No statement of a stress, accent or tone system for Kyak or any cluster language: the thesis is a segment-level comparison (consonant/vowel inventories, 103 cognate sets, 23 consonant + 6 vowel correspondence sets) and the word 'tone' occurs once in prose, about Dza/Joole Nyawo (p. 22).
